nameStory: Hemp agrimony gets its name from its deeply divided leaves that look remarkably similar to those of hemp (Cannabis), though the two plants are completely unrelated. The 'agrimony' part refers to its medicinal history, as it was once grouped with the true agrimonies that were used in folk medicine. This is actually a case of mistaken botanical identity that stuck in the common name!
description: Hemp agrimony is a robust perennial wildflower that can grow quite tall and impressive in wet spots. It produces clusters of small, fluffy pinkish-purple flowers that create a soft, cloud-like appearance from a distance. The plant has distinctive palm-shaped leaves that are deeply divided into finger-like segments. As a European native that occasionally escapes from gardens, it's quite rare in New England but unmistakable when you find it.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive palm-shaped leaves divided into 3-5 narrow, toothed segments that feel slightly rough to the touch and really do look like marijuana leaves

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, flat-topped clusters of tiny pinkish-purple flowers that feel soft and fuzzy, each individual flower head containing only disc florets with no petals

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, sturdy perennial that forms clumps in wet areas, with strong stems that feel substantial and don't break easily when bent

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found in consistently moist to wet soils near streams, ponds, or in marshy areas where few other tall wildflowers thrive

habitat: In New England, hemp agrimony is most likely found in wet meadows, along stream banks, or near pond edges where the soil stays consistently moist. It prefers rich, fertile soils in lowland areas and may occasionally appear near gardens where it has escaped cultivation. Look for it in the same types of wet habitats where you'd find native bonesets and joe-pye weeds.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with the characteristic palm-shaped leaves becoming visible early, making identification possible even before flowering.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with the distinctive pinkish-purple flower clusters fully developed and most attractive to butterflies and other pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to brown seed heads with fluffy white seeds, while leaves may turn yellowish before dying back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level, leaving no above-ground parts for winter identification.

funFact: Hemp agrimony is like a butterfly magnet on steroids – it's so irresistibly attractive to butterflies that gardeners sometimes call it 'European buddleia' for its ability to draw dozens of different butterfly species to a single plant, often with multiple butterflies feeding on one flower cluster at the same time!
confusionNotes: The palm-shaped leaves immediately separate hemp agrimony from all native New England bonesets, which have simple, undivided leaves. If you see what looks like a boneset with marijuana-shaped leaves, you've found hemp agrimony!
contextualKnowledge: Don't worry – despite the hemp-like leaves, this plant is completely unrelated to marijuana and has no psychoactive properties whatsoever. The leaf similarity is purely coincidental, and hemp agrimony belongs to the daisy family while true hemp is in an entirely different plant family.
compareHints: Hemp agrimony stands out immediately from all native New England Eupatorium species because of its deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves – every other boneset in our region has simple, undivided leaves. The pinkish-purple flowers are also more colorful than most native bonesets, which tend toward white or very pale pink. Think of it as the exotic cousin that's trying a bit too hard to stand out at the family reunion.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Eupatorium relatives, common boneset is the only one with perfoliate leaves where the stem pierces through the leaf base.

Among the bonesets, hyssopleaf thoroughwort stands out immediately for its extremely narrow leaves—while common boneset has broad, wrinkled leaves that clasp the stem, and rough boneset has lance-shaped leaves, this species looks almost grass-like.

Among the boneset family, rough boneset stands out for its notably hairy, rough-textured leaves and stems, while common boneset has distinctive leaves that appear "perforated" by the stem passing through them.
Among the boneset family, late boneset stands out for its very late bloom time and alternate leaf arrangement.

Among the many boneset species, upland boneset is distinguished by its narrow, stalkless leaves that don't wrap around the stem like common boneset, and its preference for dry habitats unlike most other bonesets.
Unlike common boneset which has leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, New England boneset has clearly separate opposite leaves.
Among the boneset family, tall boneset stands out with its alternate leaf arrangement (most other bonesets have opposite leaves) and its particularly dense, flat-topped flower clusters.
Among its boneset relatives, roundleaf thoroughwort is the wetland specialist with the roundest, softest leaves.
Among its boneset relatives in New England, dogfennel is unmistakable due to its incredibly fine, thread-like leaves - all other Eupatorium species have broad, simple leaves.
Unlike common boneset which has distinctive perfoliate leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, Torrey's eupatorium has narrow, separate leaves.
Unlike common boneset with its perforated leaves that wrap around the stem, veined thoroughwort has clearly separate opposite leaves.
